mean: freedoms and fair treatment that every person can claim by law
ex: Knowing her rights as a consumer, Meena refused to pay more than the MRP printed on the bottle.
ex2: The workers' union in Surat held a meeting to explain their rights about overtime pay and weekly leave.
note: India's Constitution lists the Fundamental Rights in Part III. Do not confuse with 'rites' (religious ceremonies).

mean: a person who legally belongs to a country
ex: Every citizen over eighteen can vote, whether they live in Ladakh or Lakshadweep.
ex2: As a citizen, Joseph felt he should report the broken traffic signal instead of just complaining about it.
note: 'Senior citizen' is very common in India for people over 60; 'older people' is also widely used abroad.

mean: dishonest use of power, such as taking bribes
ex: When the clerk asked for cash to move her file, Farzana reported the corruption to the vigilance office.
ex2: The state cricket association promised an inquiry after a news report exposed corruption in the sale of match tickets.

mean: a public act that shows strong disagreement with something
ex: Students held a silent protest outside the college gate against the sudden fee hike.
ex2: Fishermen in Kochi held a protest at the harbour against the sudden rise in diesel prices.
note: Noun: PROH-test. Verb: pruh-TEST. In British English you 'protest against' something; Americans often drop 'against'.

mean: a group of people who live together or share something in common
ex: After the Chennai floods, the whole community cooked together for families who had lost their homes.
ex2: Before the fishing season, the whole community of the coastal village repaired the boats and nets together.
note: In Indian usage 'community' often means a religious or social group; elsewhere it usually means a neighbourhood or shared interest.

mean: openness, so people can see how decisions are made and money spent
ex: For transparency, the gram panchayat painted its yearly spending on the wall outside its office.
ex2: Parents demanded transparency about the school fee hike and asked exactly where the extra money would go.
note: India's Right to Information Act (2005) lets citizens ask for government records; it is a key transparency tool.

mean: people's health and well-being, and the help given to protect it
ex: The mid-day meal is one of India's largest welfare schemes, feeding millions of schoolchildren every day.
ex2: An animal welfare group in Jaipur feeds stray dogs and runs a free clinic for injured cows.
note: One l: welfare, not 'wellfare'. A 'welfare state' gives citizens health care, pensions and support.

mean: one-sided information spread to push people towards a belief
ex: Our history teacher showed propaganda posters printed by both sides during the Second World War.
ex2: Before the election, the family WhatsApp group filled up with propaganda from every side, and Babu Mama forwarded all of it.
note: Every system produces it: governments, parties, companies, activists. Persuasion becomes propaganda when it hides or twists facts.

mean: the officials and rules that run a government or big organisation
ex: Getting a new ration card meant weeks of bureaucracy: four forms, three offices and one missing stamp.
ex2: The startup founder said his real enemy was bureaucracy: one licence needed signatures from seven departments.
note: Neutral meaning: the system of officials. Often used negatively for slow rules. Spelling: bureau + cracy.

mean: officially stopping books, films or news that authorities find unacceptable
ex: The film board's cut of a single scene started a long debate on censorship at our Kolkata adda.
ex2: When the warden banned certain magazines from the hostel common room, students called it censorship and wrote to the principal.
note: Self-censorship means staying silent out of fear. Not the same as 'censure', which means strong official criticism.

mean: strong disagreement with an official or majority view
ex: At the housing society meeting, Mrs Iyer recorded her dissent over the plan to cut down the old banyan tree.
ex2: In a healthy dressing room, a junior cricketer's dissent is heard by the captain, not punished.
note: Judges write a 'dissent' when they disagree with the majority ruling. Do not confuse with 'descent' (going down).

mean: treating someone unfairly because of their group, such as gender or religion
ex: Ananya filed a complaint when she learned male colleagues were paid more for the same work, calling it discrimination.
ex2: Refusing to rent a flat to someone because of their surname or food habits is discrimination, yet many tenants still face it.
note: Say 'discrimination against women', not 'discrimination on women'. The verb is 'discriminate against'.

mean: split into two opposite groups that strongly disagree
ex: The family WhatsApp group became so polarised over the new flyover that cousins stopped replying to each other.
ex2: The hostel was polarised over the new mess menu: half loved the millet rotis, half wanted the old food back.
note: British and Indian spelling: polarised; American: polarized. The word describes the split, not who caused it.

mean: pushed to the edge of society, with little power or voice
ex: The NGO in Odisha runs evening classes for children from marginalised fishing families.
ex2: The community radio station in Bundelkhand gives marginalised women farmers a voice on local issues.
note: 'Marginal' means small or minor; 'marginalised' means pushed aside by others.

mean: an advantage some people have and others do not, often from birth
ex: English-medium schooling and a laptop were a privilege that most students in Rohit's village never had.
ex2: A quiet room to study in is a privilege that many board exam students in crowded homes do not have.
note: Spelt without a d, not 'priviledge'. Also an honour: 'It is a privilege to speak here.'

mean: fairness that gives each person what they need to reach a fair result
ex: Under its equity plan, the school gave extra coaching to first-generation learners instead of equal hours to everyone.
ex2: Health equity means a mother in a remote Assam village should get the same care as one in a city hospital.
note: Equality gives everyone the same; equity adjusts for need. People reasonably debate which fits each case. In finance, equity means shares.

mean: giving jobs or favours to relatives instead of the most able person
ex: When the owner's nephew became manager over senior staff, the Pune office quietly grumbled about nepotism.
ex2: Film fans complained of nepotism when yet another star's son landed a big role in his very first film.
note: Nepotism favours relatives; favouring friends and allies is 'cronyism'.

mean: politics that claims to speak for ordinary people against a powerful elite
ex: On the news debate, one economist called pre-election loan waivers populism while another called them needed relief.
ex2: In the college debate, Imran argued that populism grows when people feel ignored by experts and officials.
note: Found on both left and right. Critics use it as an insult; supporters say it means listening to ordinary people.

mean: not tied to any religion; in India, treating all religions equally
ex: The Preamble describes India as a secular republic; the word was added to it in 1976.
ex2: Our school follows a secular calendar, with holidays for Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Guru Nanak Jayanti and Buddha Purnima.
note: In India it usually means equal respect for all religions; in the West, separating religion from the state. Also just 'non-religious'.

mean: serious public talk and writing about a subject
ex: A speaker at the Jaipur Literature Festival said ten-second clips now shape public discourse more than long articles do.
ex2: Doctors worry that health discourse on social media is driven by home remedies, not by research.
note: Formal. 'Discourse' is the whole conversation a society has on a topic, not one chat.

mean: a leader who wins support by stirring anger and fear, not reason
ex: Our civics teacher said a demagogue offers crowds a simple enemy instead of a real solution.
ex2: In history class, we read how a demagogue in 1930s Europe blamed one community for every problem the country had.
note: Always critical. Calling someone a demagogue is itself a strong claim that needs evidence.

mean: to take away someone's right to vote or to have a say
ex: Holding the vote on harvest day could disenfranchise farmers who cannot leave their fields.
ex2: Moving the polling booth ten kilometres away would disenfranchise elderly villagers who cannot travel that far.
note: Also used loosely: feeling disenfranchised means feeling you have no say. The opposite is 'enfranchise'.

mean: support from a powerful person, often jobs or favours in return for loyalty
ex: Under royal patronage, Thanjavur painters and Carnatic musicians flourished for generations.
ex2: For decades, the textile mill owner's patronage kept the town's cricket club and its library alive.
note: Positive for the arts; negative in politics, where jobs go to loyal supporters instead of the most able.

mean: freedom from punishment, even after doing wrong
ex: The builder dumped debris into the lake with impunity, sure that no inspector would ever come.
ex2: Bikers in the colony jumped red lights with impunity until the traffic police put up cameras.
note: Almost always in 'with impunity'. Not 'immunity', which means legal protection or resistance to disease.

mean: strong control or influence of one group or country over others
ex: For years, Australia's hegemony over world cricket made every other team look ordinary.
ex2: Small Indian apps struggle against the hegemony of a few global tech giants that decide what we see online.
note: Also said heh-GEM-uh-nee. 'Cultural hegemony' means one group's ideas come to seem natural to everyone.

mean: answering criticism by pointing to someone else's wrongs instead
ex: Asked about potholes, the city spokesperson used whataboutism, listing the rival city's potholes instead.
ex2: When Riya said her brother hadn't washed the dishes, he answered with whataboutism: 'What about your unmade bed?'
note: Every side uses it. Pointing out a double standard can be fair; whataboutism dodges the original question.

mean: being equal in rights, chances and treatment
ex: The Constitution promises equality before the law, whether you are a minister's son or a mill worker's.
ex2: At the gurdwara langar, everyone sits on the floor together, which Harpreet calls equality in practice.
note: Equality gives everyone the same; 'equity' gives each person what they need to reach a fair result.

mean: the state of being very poor
ex: Free school meals stopped many children in Jharkhand from dropping out because of poverty.
ex2: Raised in poverty in a one-room chawl, Salim saved for years to open his own tailoring shop.
note: Indian news often says 'below the poverty line' (BPL), the official term for the poorest families.

mean: to offer to do a job without being paid or forced
ex: During the Kerala floods, fishermen from Kollam came to volunteer, rescuing families in their own boats.
ex2: Every Sunday, Neha and her college friends volunteer at an old age home in Dehradun.
note: Also a noun: 'a volunteer'. The stress is at the end: vol-un-TEER.

mean: a written request, signed by many people, asking officials to act
ex: Over two thousand residents signed a petition asking the corporation to fix the dead streetlights on their road.
ex2: After the cyclone, parents sent a petition to the school board asking for the exams to be moved.
note: In court news, a petition is a formal request to a judge, as in a PIL (public interest litigation).

mean: an unfair gap between groups in money, chances or rights
ex: In Gurugram, glass towers standing beside workers' tin sheds show the city's sharp inequality.
ex2: The report on girls' schooling showed inequality between districts: some schools had libraries, others had no toilets.

mean: a person who campaigns hard to change laws, rules or opinions
ex: A young activist from Ladakh cycled from school to school, teaching children how to save glacier water.
ex2: Ramesh became an activist after builders dumped debris into the lake behind his Bengaluru colony.
note: A social worker gives help directly; an activist campaigns to change laws or public opinion.

mean: a fixed, too-simple idea about what a whole group is like
ex: The film breaks the stereotype that people from small towns cannot speak confident English.
ex2: By topping the state in maths, Priya broke the stereotype that girls are weaker with numbers.

mean: open to and welcoming everyone, leaving no group out
ex: The new metro stations are more inclusive, with ramps, lifts and Braille signs for disabled travellers.
ex2: The college fest became more inclusive once it added sign-language interpreters and events in Hindi and Tamil.
note: 'Inclusive of' also means 'including': Rs 500, inclusive of GST.

mean: ordinary people at the local level, not the leaders
ex: The women's self-help group started at the grassroots, with ten members saving fifty rupees a week.
ex2: The cricket academy looks for talent at the grassroots, watching tennis-ball matches on village maidans.
note: Often used like an adjective: a grassroots campaign. Write it as one word.

mean: about a town or city and the duties of the people living there
ex: A poster at Howrah station reminded passengers that civic sense means not spitting paan on the walls.
ex2: Voting in the ward election is a civic duty, so Ammi went to the booth before cooking lunch.
note: 'Civic sense' is common Indian English for good public behaviour; a 'civic body' is the city corporation.

mean: shame or disapproval that society attaches to something
ex: Talking openly about therapy helps remove the stigma around mental health in Indian families.
ex2: Health workers in Bihar are fighting the stigma around leprosy so that patients come forward early.
note: Usually 'the stigma of', 'the stigma around' or 'the stigma attached to' something.

mean: a big, unfair difference between two things or groups
ex: There is a huge disparity between the hospitals of Mumbai and those in rural Vidarbha.
ex2: The pay disparity between men and women cricketers was debated for years before match fees were made equal.
note: More formal than 'gap'; common in news about income, health and regions.

mean: strongly supporting one side, without being fair
ex: Viewers complained that the news anchor was openly partisan, cutting off one panellist and praising the other.
ex2: As umpire in the colony match, Joshi Uncle was so partisan that even his own team felt embarrassed.
note: Also a noun for a strong supporter. In wartime history, partisans were fighters against an occupying army.

mean: unity and support between people who share an aim
ex: Auto drivers across Pune switched off their engines for an hour in solidarity with a colleague who was attacked.
ex2: Students wore black bands in solidarity with the hostel cooks, who had not been paid for three months.

mean: doing a small thing only to look fair, without real change
ex: The company put one woman on its board for the annual report photo, but critics called it tokenism.
ex2: Students called it tokenism when the Pune college planted ten saplings on Environment Day and cut fifty trees for a car park.

mean: loud, aggressive pride in your country that is eager for a fight
ex: Before every big cricket match, some TV channels mix sport with jingoism, as if a game were a war.
ex2: Our history teacher showed how jingoism in European newspapers helped crowds cheer the start of the First World War.
note: Patriotism is love of your country; jingoism shows it by wanting to fight or insult others.
